title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
titleZh: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
author: LetThingsBeDiff
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
textRawHtml:
I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.

In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?

If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

comments.author: powvans
comments.textRawHtml:
> In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP.

If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways.

It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job.

It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast.

children.author: al_borland
children.textRawHtml:
There are also companies that do layoffs routinely. When I started where I work, they didn't. I remember the first time I experienced layoffs, it was a dark day in the office. These days, they happen at least twice per year, and that's been the trend for many years now. I've been at the company for over 2 decades now, and have watched countless rounds of layoffs happen while I retained my job. Never actually feeling like you have job security when being somewhere for 20 years is not fun, but it does highlight that they aren't always the end. On year, I was told 3 times I was getting laid off, I had meetings with HR and signed severance papers and everything... as I left the office my boss told me not to worry... that was 10 years ago. I'm still working there, that boss was laid off a few years later.

It could be that companies that historically didn't do layoffs are starting to move into the regular cadence I've been experiencing for years. To echo the parent, I don't know OP's situation, but these scenarios exist.

children.author: ChuckMcM
children.textRawHtml:
Well, in my experience that regardless of how its done, when the company asks you to leave and continues on without you, it feels like they fired you and that you were not "picked" to continue on with them. If the company dissolves after laying you off that is a different thing.

For employees its a double negative, new employers will see being laid off as "you weren't part of the top 10%" and by leaving on your own terms, "this guy's a quitter, he might quit on us too." Which is really just people trying to find excuses to not hire. When I was on the hiring rotation at Google I asked the committee once "Why do you bring these people in if you already don't think you will hire them?" The whole "Maybe they will surprise us..." rings hollow.

My advice to the folks like the OP living in the US is to use your IT experience to help folks in Active Senior kinds of communities with their IT issues. You can do it for 'free' or a nominal charge. This is an easy way to network with successful former executives who still have contacts in the industry.

children.author: eloisant
children.textRawHtml:
> new employers will see being laid off as "you weren't part of the top 10%"

No that's not the case. There are many reasons your employer decide you're the one the be laid off that are not related to performances. Maybe your salary is higher. Maybe your whole department or location is shutdown. New employers know that and don't judge laid off people.

> this guy's a quitter, he might quit on us too.

That can be true, but only if you have a short tenure in the companies you worked for. Companies might think that if you have multiple jobs with less than a year. But if you quit a company after working for at least 2/3 years, companies won't judge you for that.

children.textRawHtml:
> New employers know that and don't judge laid off people.

While nothing is universal, there are lots of companies that will absolutely not hire someone who has been laid off on the basis that they are the "scraps" or "they were cut for a reason".

It's awful but it's not exactly uncommon.
